title: Nuclear Chemistry

toc.title: 12.1 Radioactivity and the types of nuclear reaction
12.3 Nuclear equations and the shift in the periodic table
12.6 Radioisotopes: how they are made and what they are used for

html:
Nuclear chemistry is the shortest chapter in the Chemistry paper — one question in the fifty — but it is almost free marks, because the same six facts are asked year after year: which radiation penetrates most, what happens to A and Z in alpha and beta decay, what half-life means, how fission differs from fusion, which isotope is used for which job, and one line of arithmetic on carbon dating. Nothing here needs a laboratory; everything needs the table in §12.2 to be memorised exactly.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • The three radiations with charge, mass, penetration and ionising power — the two orders run in opposite directions.
  • Alpha decay: A falls by 4, Z falls by 2, the element moves two places left. Beta decay: A unchanged, Z rises by 1, one place right. Gamma: neither changes.
  • Half-life: t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda; after n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)^n, and the activity falls in exactly the same way.
  • Half-life is a nuclear property: temperature, pressure, chemical combination and physical state do not touch it.
  • Fission splits a heavy nucleus (about 200 MeV each time); fusion joins light nuclei (the Sun's reaction). Both release energy because the products are more tightly bound.
  • The isotope–use pairs: Tc-99m imaging, I-131 thyroid, Co-60 radiotherapy and sterilisation, C-14 dating.
  • Radiocarbon dating: t = (t_{1/2}/0.693)\ln(A_0/A), with the assumption that the ^{14}C : ^{12}C ratio in living things has stayed constant.

12.1 Radioactivity and the types of nuclear reaction

What radioactivity is

Radioactivity

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of particles or electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus of an unstable atom, accompanied by the change of that atom into a different nuclide. It is a nuclear change, not a chemical one: the electrons are not rearranged, the nucleus itself breaks up.

The nucleus is held together by the strong force, which acts over a very short range and must overcome the electrostatic repulsion of the protons. A nucleus is stable when the neutron-to-proton ratio lies in a narrow band. Outside that band it decays:

What is wrong with the nucleus What it does
too many neutrons (n/p too high) beta-minus decay: a neutron turns into a proton
too few neutrons (n/p too low) positron emission or electron capture
too heavy (large Z, whatever the ratio) alpha decay, or spontaneous fission

The history worth knowing. Henri Becquerel found in 1896 that a uranium salt darkened a photographic plate through black paper, with no exposure to light — the first observation of radioactivity. Marie and Pierre Curie separated polonium and radium from pitchblende in 1898. Rutherford named the alpha and beta rays in 1899, and Villard found the third, gamma, in 1900.

Natural radioactivity is shown by nuclides that exist in nature and decay on their own. All elements beyond bismuth (Z = 83) are radioactive, and a few lighter nuclides are too: potassium-40, rubidium-87, carbon-14 and tritium. The three natural series are headed by uranium-238, uranium-235 and thorium-232; each ends in a stable isotope of lead.

Artificial (induced) radioactivity is radioactivity in a nuclide made in the laboratory by bombarding a stable nucleus. Irène and Frédéric Joliot-Curie made the first one in 1934:

²⁷₁₃Al + ⁴₂He → ³⁰₁₅P + ¹₀n, and the phosphorus-30 produced is itself a positron emitter (half-life 2.5 min). Every radioisotope used in medicine and industry is made this way, in a nuclear reactor or a cyclotron.

Natural radioactivity Artificial radioactivity
Source of the nuclide found in nature (U-238, Th-232, K-40, C-14) made by bombarding a stable nucleus
What is emitted mostly α, β⁻ and γ α, β⁻, β⁺, γ, and often neutrons
Number of nuclides about 60 over 2,000
Energy of the radiation fixed by the parent nuclide can be chosen by choosing the reaction
Example ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He ²⁷₁₃Al + ⁴₂He → ³⁰₁₅P + ¹₀n

Nuclear reactions compared with chemical reactions

Feature Chemical reaction Nuclear reaction
What changes the arrangement of electrons and atoms the nucleus itself
New element formed? no usually yes (transmutation)
A and Z unchanged change (but the totals are conserved)
Energy per event a few eV per molecule MeV per nucleus — about a million times more
Mass conserved to any measurable precision a small mass defect appears as energy, E = \Delta m\,c^2
Rate depends on temperature, pressure, concentration, catalyst nothing external — only on the nuclide and its half-life
Example 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n

The types of nuclear reaction

  1. Radioactive decay — spontaneous: alpha, beta-minus, positron, electron capture, gamma, and spontaneous fission of very heavy nuclei.
  2. Artificial transmutation — a nucleus is struck by a projectile (α particle, proton, deuteron, neutron or a gamma photon) and changes into another nuclide. Rutherford produced the first one in 1919: ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ¹₁H.
  3. Nuclear fission — a heavy nucleus splits into two medium-sized nuclei after absorbing a neutron.
  4. Nuclear fusion — two light nuclei join to make a heavier one.
  5. Neutron capture (neutron activation) — a nucleus absorbs a neutron and becomes a heavier isotope of the same element, usually gamma-emitting: ⁵⁹₂₇Co + ¹₀n → ⁶⁰₂₇Co + γ. This is how cobalt-60 is manufactured.
"Radioactivity cannot be switched off"

A radioactive sample cannot be heated, cooled, compressed, dissolved or combined with another element to change its half-life. The decay of a given nucleus is a random event governed by the weak or strong force inside the nucleus; chemistry happens in the electron cloud, far outside. What can be changed is the chemical form, and that changes only where the isotope goes in the body or in a plant — not how fast it decays.

12.2 The three radiations

Property Alpha, α Beta, β⁻ Gamma, γ
Nature helium nucleus, ⁴₂He²⁺ fast electron from the nucleus electromagnetic wave (photon)
Charge +2 −1 0
Mass 4 u (2 protons + 2 neutrons) 1/1837 u (about 0.00055 u) zero rest mass
Speed about 0.05c (up to 0.1c) up to 0.99c c
Penetration in air 2–8 cm a few metres hundreds of metres
Stopped by a sheet of paper, skin a few mm of aluminium several cm of lead, thick concrete
Ionising power very high (about 10⁴ × gamma) moderate (about 100 × gamma) low
Deflection in an electric field towards the negative plate, slightly towards the positive plate, strongly not deflected
Effect of a magnetic field deflected deflected the other way not deflected

Alpha particle. Two protons and two neutrons, identical to a helium nucleus, emitted by heavy nuclei that have too little binding energy per nucleon. It is heavy and slow, so it rips electrons off every atom it passes — high ionising power — but it loses its energy within a few centimetres of air and is stopped by paper or the dead outer layer of skin. That makes it harmless outside the body and the most dangerous radiation inside it: an alpha emitter breathed in or swallowed deposits all its energy in a few cells. Radium watch-dial painters and radon in basements are the classic examples.

Beta particle. A fast electron created in the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ (the antineutrino, which carries away the missing energy — that is why the beta spectrum is continuous while the alpha spectrum is a set of sharp lines). The electron is not one of the orbital electrons. Beta particles are light, so they are easily deflected and moderately penetrating, and they are stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium or perspex.

Gamma ray. A high-energy photon, emitted when a nucleus left in an excited state drops to a lower state. It carries away energy but no mass and no charge, so the nuclide does not change: ⁶⁰₂₇Co* → ⁶⁰₂₇Co + γ. Gamma rays are the most penetrating of the three and the least ionising; thick lead or concrete is needed.

The two orders are opposite

Penetration: γ > β > α. Ionising power: α > β > γ. A question that asks "which radiation is most penetrating" and a question that asks "which is most ionising" have different answers — this is the single most common trap in the chapter. The reason is simple: a particle that gives up its energy quickly (strong ionisation) cannot travel far.

One line for the table

Alpha is a helium nucleus (+2, heavy, paper); beta is a nuclear electron (−1, light, aluminium); gamma is light itself (0, no mass, lead). Then remember that the heavy, charged, slow one ionises most and penetrates least.

12.3 Nuclear equations and the shift in the periodic table

The two conservation rules

In every nuclear equation two totals are conserved:

  1. Nucleon number A (mass number): the sum of the superscripts is the same on both sides.
  2. Charge Z (atomic number): the sum of the subscripts, including the charge of an electron written as −1, is the same on both sides.

Mass itself is not exactly conserved — a tiny amount becomes energy — but A and Z always are. Balance A first, then Z; the element symbol then follows from Z.

Alpha decay

²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He

Check: 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2. The daughter has A smaller by 4 and Z smaller by 2, so it sits two places to the left in the periodic table. Two more examples:

²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He (radium → radon, the gas that seeps into basements)

²¹⁸₈₄Po → ²¹⁴₈₂Pb + ⁴₂He

Beta-minus decay

¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e

Check: 14 = 14 + 0 and 6 = 7 + (-1). A is unchanged, Z rises by one, so the element moves one place to the right. The product has the same mass number as the parent — the two are isobars. More examples:

³²₁₅P → ³²₁₆S + ⁰₋₁e (the phosphorus-32 used as a tracer)

²¹⁴₈₂Pb → ²¹⁴₈₃Bi + ⁰₋₁e

Positron emission and electron capture

A nucleus with too few neutrons can convert a proton into a neutron in two ways.

Positron emission — a positive electron leaves the nucleus:

²²₁₁Na → ²²₁₀Ne + ⁰₊₁e

Check: 22 = 22 + 0 and 11 = 10 + 1. Here Z falls by one, so the element moves one place to the left. This is the decay of the isotopes used in PET scanning.

Electron capture — the nucleus grabs one of its own inner electrons:

⁴⁰₁₉K + ⁰₋₁e → ⁴⁰₁₈Ar

Check: 40 = 40 and 19 - 1 = 18. The result is the same as positron emission: Z falls by one, A unchanged. Electron capture competes with positron emission whenever the energy available is small.

Gamma emission

⁶⁰₂₇Co → ⁶⁰₂₇Co + γ (or, written fully, ⁶⁰₂₇Co → ⁶⁰₂₇Co + ⁰₀γ)

The asterisk marks a nucleus in an excited state. Nothing about A or Z changes, so gamma emission alone never produces a new element. It usually follows alpha or beta decay, when the daughter is left excited. Technetium-99m is the important case: the "m" means metastable, an excited state that lasts long enough (6 hours) to be used in a hospital.

Decay Change in A Change in Z Periodic-table shift Parent and daughter are
alpha, α −4 −2 two places left different elements, A differs by 4
beta-minus, β⁻ 0 +1 one place right isobars
positron, β⁺ 0 −1 one place left isobars
electron capture 0 −1 one place left isobars
gamma, γ 0 0 no shift isomers (same nuclide, different energy)

Finding the daughter nuclide

Problem. Radium-226 emits an alpha particle. Write the equation and state where the daughter sits in the periodic table relative to radium.

Solution. An alpha particle is ⁴₂He, so the daughter has A = 226 - 4 = 222 and Z = 88 - 2 = 86. Element 86 is radon: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He. Radon is two places to the left of radium (group 18 instead of group 2), and still in period 6.

How many alpha and beta particles in a series?

Problem. The uranium series starts at ²³⁸₉₂U and ends at ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb. How many alpha and how many beta particles are emitted in the whole series?

Solution. Only alpha decay changes A, and each alpha removes 4: (238 - 206)/4 = 8 alpha particles. Those 8 alphas remove 8 \times 2 = 16 units of charge, taking Z from 92 to 76. The final Z is 82, which is 6 more, and each beta raises Z by 1: 6 beta particles. Answer: 8 α and 6 β.

The three mistakes that cost the mark
  • In beta decay Z goes up by one, not down, and A does not change. The electron leaves with a charge of −1, so the nucleus must gain +1 to keep the charge balance.
  • In alpha decay A falls by 4, not 2, and Z by 2 — not by 4.
  • Gamma emission changes nothing: an option that says "gamma decay produces a new element" is always wrong. If a question asks which decay leaves A and Z unchanged, the answer is gamma.

12.4 The decay law and half-life

The law

Radioactive decay is random: we cannot say when one particular nucleus will decay, but in a large sample the rate is proportional to the number of nuclei present. With N nuclei at time t and decay constant \lambda (the probability of decay per nucleus per second):

\frac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}

N_0 is the number at t = 0, N the number left at time t, and \lambda has the unit s⁻¹ (or y⁻¹ if t is in years). Because the activity A is proportional to N (A = \lambda N), the activity obeys exactly the same law:

A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}

Half-life t_{1/2} is the time in which half of the nuclei in a sample decay. Put N = N_0/2:

\frac{N_0}{2} = N_0 e^{-\lambda t_{1/2}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ln 2 = \lambda t_{1/2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}

That single relation is worth more marks than the rest of the chapter, because it converts a question about \lambda into a question about t_{1/2} and back.

Counting half-lives is faster than using e. If a time t contains n = t/t_{1/2} half-lives, then

\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n}, \qquad \text{fraction decayed} = 1 - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n}

The same fraction applies to mass of the isotope, to number of atoms and to activity — but not to the total mass of the sample, because the daughter nuclei stay behind.

Three half-lives, worked the MCQ way

Problem. A source contains 64 mg of a radioisotope of half-life 12 hours. What mass of that isotope remains after 36 hours, and what fraction has decayed?

Solution. n = 36/12 = 3 half-lives. Remaining = 64 \times (1/2)^3 = 64/8 = 8 mg. Fraction decayed = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8 = 87.5 %. Note that the answer is not zero and not "64 − 3 × 32": halving is not subtracting.

Half-life from a fraction

Problem. A radioisotope has fallen to 1/16 of its original activity in 60 days. Find its half-life.

Solution. (1/2)^n = 1/16 gives n = 4 half-lives. t_{1/2} = 60/4 = 15 days.

The decay constant of carbon-14

Problem. Find \lambda for ^{14}C (t_{1/2} = 5730 y), and the time for 90 % of a sample to decay.

Solution. \lambda = 0.693/5730 = 1.21 \times 10^{-4} y⁻¹. For 90 % decayed, 10 % remains: t = \ln(10)/\lambda = 2.303/(1.21 \times 10^{-4}) \approx 1.9 × 10⁴ y. That is why carbon dating is unreliable beyond about 40,000–50,000 years: so little ^{14}C is left that contamination by a speck of modern carbon ruins the count.

Units of radioactivity

Unit Symbol What it measures Size
becquerel Bq activity: decays per second 1 Bq = 1 decay s⁻¹ (SI unit)
curie Ci activity 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq (activity of 1 g of radium-226)
rutherford Rd activity 1 Rd = 10⁶ Bq (rarely used)
gray Gy absorbed dose 1 Gy = 1 J of energy per kg of tissue
sievert Sv equivalent dose (biological harm) 1 Sv = 1 Gy × quality factor (α: 20, β and γ: 1)
Four statements that are false
  • "After one half-life all the atoms have decayed." No — half remain; after n half-lives, (1/2)^n remain.
  • "The half-life of a sample depends on how much of it there is." No — t_{1/2} is a constant of the nuclide; a 1 g sample and a 1 kg sample both halve in the same time.
  • "Cooling a radioactive source slows its decay." No — temperature has no effect.
  • "The activity falls to half, so the mass of the sample falls to half." Only the mass of that isotope halves; the daughter nuclei remain in the sample.

12.5 Nuclear fission and fusion

Fission

Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two medium-sized nuclei of comparable mass, with the release of two or three neutrons and a large amount of energy. It is started by absorbing a slow (thermal) neutron, because the neutron has no charge and so faces no Coulomb barrier:

²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n + about 200 MeV

Check the balance: 235 + 1 = 236 on the left and 141 + 92 + 3 = 236 on the right; 92 = 56 + 36. Barium and krypton are only one possible pair — the same uranium nucleus can split in dozens of ways (xenon-144 and strontium-90, caesium-137 and rubidium-95, and so on), which is why reactor waste is such a mixture.

The three neutrons can split three more nuclei, which release nine neutrons, and so on: a chain reaction. If on average fewer than one neutron from each fission causes another fission, the reaction dies out (sub-critical); exactly one, it runs steadily (critical); more than one, it grows explosively (super-critical). The critical mass is the smallest mass that can sustain a chain reaction — for uranium-235 it is a few tens of kilograms, depending on shape and the moderator around it.

In a reactor the chain reaction is held at exactly one neutron per fission:

Part Material Job
fuel rods enriched U-235 (a few per cent) sealed in zirconium or steel supply the fissionable nuclei
moderator heavy water, ordinary water or graphite slow fast neutrons to thermal speed (slow neutrons fission U-235 far more readily)
control rods boron, cadmium or hafnium absorb surplus neutrons; pushed in to slow the reaction, pulled out to speed it
coolant water, heavy water, liquid sodium or CO₂ carry the heat to the steam generator
shielding thick concrete and lead stop the neutrons and gamma rays

Note that the moderator and the control rods do opposite jobs: the moderator slows neutrons (making them more effective), the control rods remove them.

Fusion

Fusion is the joining of two light nuclei into one heavier nucleus. It is the reaction of the Sun and of every star, and it powers the hydrogen bomb. The easiest reaction to ignite is deuterium + tritium:

²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV

and the Sun's main sequence burns hydrogen through the proton–proton chain, whose net result is 4¹₁H → ⁴₂He + 2⁰₊₁e + energy (about 26.7 MeV). Fusion needs temperatures of the order of 10⁷–10⁸ K: the nuclei must be moving fast enough to come within about 10⁻¹⁵ m, against the electrostatic repulsion of their protons.

Why both release energy

The binding energy per nucleon rises steeply through the light elements, peaks at iron-56 (8.79 MeV per nucleon) and then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV per nucleon at uranium. Moving towards the peak releases energy, and it can be done from either side: splitting uranium moves its nucleons to more tightly bound middle-mass nuclei (fission), and joining hydrogen moves its nucleons to helium (fusion). Iron-56 sits at the bottom of the energy valley, so neither fission nor fusion of iron releases energy.

Fission Fusion
What happens one heavy nucleus splits into two two light nuclei join into one
Fuel U-235, Pu-239 (scarce, mined) deuterium and tritium (deuterium is abundant in sea water)
Trigger a slow neutron extremely high temperature (10⁷–10⁸ K)
Energy per event about 200 MeV about 17.6 MeV for D–T
Energy per kilogram of fuel large much larger (about four times fission, gram for gram)
Products radioactive fission fragments, long-lived waste helium, and a neutron; little long-lived waste
Status commercial power stations since the 1950s experimental (ITER); not yet a power source
Where it happens naturally not on Earth naturally (reactors and bombs only) in the Sun and stars
Fission and fusion are not the same word with two spellings

Fission = splitting (think scissors), heavy nucleus, needs a neutron, works at room temperature, produces radioactive waste. Fusion = joining (think fuse), light nuclei, needs millions of kelvin, produces helium. An option that says "the Sun's energy comes from fission" is a standard wrong key. Also: both release energy, but only fission is used in today's power stations.

12.6 Radioisotopes: how they are made and what they are used for

How a radioisotope is made

  1. Neutron bombardment in a reactor. The nucleus absorbs a neutron and becomes a heavier isotope of the same element, usually emitting a gamma ray. This is cheap and gives neutron-rich isotopes, which decay by beta emission: ⁵⁹₂₇Co + ¹₀n → ⁶⁰₂₇Co + γ; ³²₁₆S + ¹₀n → ³²₁₅P + ¹₁H (a (n,p) reaction).
  2. Charged-particle bombardment in a cyclotron. Protons, deuterons or alpha particles are accelerated and fired at a target; the product is usually proton-rich and decays by positron emission or electron capture. This is how short-lived hospital isotopes are made on site: ¹⁸₈O + ¹₁H → ¹⁸₉F + ¹₀n gives fluorine-18 for PET scans, and the classic teaching example of the first artificial radioisotope is ²⁷₁₃Al + ⁴₂He → ³⁰₁₅P + ¹₀n.
  3. Separation from fission products. A reactor's spent fuel contains a whole periodic table of isotopes; ⁹⁰Sr, ¹³¹I and ¹³⁷Cs are recovered from it.
  4. From a generator. A long-lived parent is shipped to the hospital and its short-lived daughter is "milked" on the spot: ⁹⁹₄₂Mo (66 h) → ⁹⁹₄₃Tc* (6 h). This is the source of nearly all technetium-99m used in the world.

The isotope–use pairs the paper tests

Isotope Half-life Radiation Main use
Tc-99m 6 h γ (140 keV) imaging of bone, heart, kidney, thyroid, lungs — the workhorse of nuclear medicine
I-131 8.0 d β⁻ and γ thyroid imaging and treatment of hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer
I-123 13 h γ thyroid imaging with a lower dose than I-131
Co-60 5.27 y β⁻ and γ (1.17, 1.33 MeV) radiotherapy of cancer; sterilising syringes and surgical instruments; food irradiation; industrial radiography of welds
C-14 5730 y β⁻ radiocarbon dating; tracing carbon in photosynthesis
P-32 14.3 d β⁻ tracing DNA and RNA; fertiliser-uptake studies in plants; treatment of polycythaemia
Fe-59 44.5 d β⁻ and γ tracing iron in blood and the study of anaemia
Na-24 15 h γ detecting leaks in underground pipes; measuring blood flow
Am-241 432 y α household smoke detectors (ionises the air in the chamber)
Sr-90 28.8 y β⁻ thickness gauges; superficial radiotherapy of the eye
U-235 7.0 × 10⁸ y α reactor fuel; uranium–lead dating of rocks
K-40 1.25 × 10⁹ y β⁻ and γ potassium–argon dating of rocks
H-3 (tritium) 12.3 y β⁻ tracer in water and in reaction mechanisms; luminous paint

Why Tc-99m dominates medicine. It emits a single gamma ray of 140 keV — energetic enough to leave the body, gentle enough to be imaged by a gamma camera; it has no beta emission, so the patient's tissue dose is small; its 6-hour half-life is long enough to prepare and inject but short enough to disappear in a day; and it can be attached to many different carrier molecules that go to bone, heart muscle or kidney. A generator in the hospital supplies it fresh each morning.

Uses by field

  • Medicine. Imaging (Tc-99m, I-123, F-18, Ga-67); therapy (I-131 for thyroid, Co-60 and linear accelerators for deep tumours, Sr-90 for the eye, Y-90 for liver tumours); sterilising heat-sensitive instruments and gloves with Co-60 gamma rays; radioimmunoassay of hormones.
  • Agriculture. Tracing the uptake of phosphorus and nitrogen fertilisers (P-32, N-15); following the path of water and pesticides in soil; mutation breeding of new crop varieties (gamma irradiation of seeds); preserving onions and potatoes by stopping sprouting; sterilising male insects to control pests.
  • Industry. Thickness gauges for paper, plastic and sheet metal (absorption of beta or gamma rays); level and density gauges; leak detection in buried pipelines (Na-24); testing welds and castings by gamma radiography (Co-60, Ir-192); smoke detectors (Am-241); tracing wear in engine parts; static elimination.
  • Archaeology and geology. Carbon-14 for organic remains up to about 50,000 years; uranium–lead for the age of the Earth and of rocks; potassium–argon for volcanic rock; thermoluminescence for pottery (a different technique, not C-14).
  • Energy and research. U-235 as fuel; tracers in reaction-mechanism studies (isotopic labelling with D, C-14, O-18).
Which isotope for which job

Learn the four the paper returns to: Tc-99m — imaging; I-131 — thyroid; Co-60 — radiotherapy and sterilisation; C-14 — dating. Distractors usually swap them (Co-60 for imaging, I-131 for dating). Also note that I-131 treats as well as images, because it emits beta particles as well as gamma; Tc-99m only images, because it is a pure gamma emitter.

12.7 Radiocarbon dating

Where the carbon-14 comes from

Cosmic rays knock neutrons out of atoms in the upper atmosphere, and those neutrons react with nitrogen:

¹⁴₇N + ¹₀n → ¹⁴₆C + ¹₁H

The carbon-14 is oxidised to ¹⁴CO₂, mixes with ordinary ¹²CO₂, and enters plants by photosynthesis and animals by eating. While an organism is alive its carbon is exchanged with the atmosphere continuously, so the ratio ¹⁴C : ¹²C in its tissues stays at the atmospheric value — about 1 : 10¹². When it dies, the exchange stops. The ¹⁴C already inside decays with a half-life of 5730 years, and the ¹²C stays put, so the ratio falls. Measure the ratio (or the beta activity) and the time since death follows.

t = \frac{t_{1/2}}{0.693}\,\ln\frac{A_0}{A} = \frac{t_{1/2}}{0.693}\,\ln\frac{N_0}{N}

A_0 is the activity of a living sample of the same material, A the activity now, and t_{1/2} = 5730 y. For a whole number of half-lives the logarithm is not needed: just count the halvings.

Carbon dating with a whole number of half-lives

Problem. A wooden beam from a temple gives a ¹⁴C activity that is 25 % of that of living wood. Find its age (t_{1/2} = 5730 y).

Solution. 25\% = 1/4 = (1/2)^2, so 2 half-lives have passed: t = 2 \times 5730 = 11,460 years.

Carbon dating with a fraction that is not a simple power

Problem. A bone sample has 35 % of the ¹⁴C activity of living bone. Find its age (t_{1/2} = 5730 y, \ln(1/0.35) = 1.05).

Solution. t = (5730/0.693) \times 1.05 = 8268 \times 1.05 \approx 8,700 years. Always check the answer against the halving picture: 35 % lies between 50 % (5730 y) and 25 % (11,460 y), so an answer near 8,700 y is reasonable, while 5,730 y or 17,190 y is not.

The assumption it rests on

The whole method assumes that the proportion of ¹⁴C in the atmosphere — and therefore in living tissue — has been constant over the period being dated. That requires the cosmic-ray flux to have been constant, the Earth's magnetic field (which shields us from cosmic rays) to have been constant, and the amount of fossil carbon burnt (which dilutes ¹⁴C) to have been negligible. Tree-ring and coral calibration curves correct for the small known variations. The method also assumes that the sample has stayed a closed system — no carbon added or lost after death (no contamination by modern carbon, no exchange with groundwater) — and that the half-life is accurately known.

Question Answer
What is dated? material that was once alive: wood, charcoal, bone, shell, peat, cloth, paper
What is measured? the ¹⁴C activity (or the ¹⁴C : ¹²C ratio) left in it
Half-life used 5730 years (the "Libby" value; the modern measured value is 5700 ± 30 y)
Useful range about 100 to 50,000 years (after 9 half-lives too little is left)
Key assumption the ¹⁴C : ¹²C ratio in living things has been constant
Cannot date rocks, metals, pottery itself (only organic matter in or on it)
Carbon dating dates the death of the organism

It does not date the age of the Earth, of a rock, or of a metal tool. A wooden handle on a bronze axe gives the age of the tree, not of the metal. And a sample contaminated with a little modern carbon — a fingerprint, mould, or museum glue — will read far too young, because modern carbon has the full ¹⁴C level.

12.8 Hazards and safe handling

What radiation does to tissue

Ionising radiation removes electrons from molecules. In the body it ionises water, producing free radicals (OH•, H•) that attack DNA. A cell whose DNA is badly damaged either dies or reproduces with a mutation. The effects are grouped as:

  • Somatic (in the exposed person): reddening and burns of the skin, nausea and radiation sickness at high dose, cataracts, and after a delay of years, leukaemia and other cancers.
  • Genetic (in the person's children): mutations in the germ cells, which may cause birth defects. These have been shown in animals and are assumed in humans.
  • Deterministic effects (burns, sickness) appear only above a threshold dose; stochastic effects (cancer) have no threshold — any dose adds a small probability.

The average person receives about 2–3 mSv a year from natural sources, of which the largest single contributor is radon gas seeping from the ground into houses.

The rules of safe handling

Principle What it means in practice
Shielding keep sources in lead pots; use lead glass or concrete walls for gamma; perspex for beta (lead would produce X-rays by bremsstrahlung)
Distance dose falls as 1/r^2; use long tongs and never hold a source in the hand
Time plan the work, then do it quickly; the dose is rate × time
Containment work with open sources in a fume cupboard or glove box, on a tray with absorbent paper
Monitoring film badge or TLD dosimeter for every worker; Geiger–Müller counter to check benches and hands
Labelling and records trefoil sign, isotope, activity and date on every container; a log of receipts and disposals
Disposal solid waste in shielded drums, liquid waste in approved sinks or drums, gaseous waste through filters; short-lived waste is left to decay
Personal rules no eating, drinking or smoking in the lab; gloves; wash hands; pregnant staff avoid work with open sources
Medical use the smallest activity that gives a diagnostic image; a pure gamma emitter such as Tc-99m; the isotope is chosen to leave the body quickly
The alpha paradox, and the beta shielding trap

An alpha source in a sealed tube is almost harmless — a sheet of paper stops it. The same isotope swallowed or inhaled is the most damaging of all, because all of its energy is deposited in a few micrometres of living tissue. That is why radon, an alpha emitter, is a serious indoor hazard, and why plutonium is dangerous mainly as dust. Conversely, beta sources should be shielded with perspex or aluminium, not lead: the heavy lead nucleus decelerates the electron and converts its energy into X-rays (bremsstrahlung), which are harder to stop than the beta particles themselves.

Chapter summary

  • Write the two bookkeeping integers (A, Z) honestly and every nuclear equation, including series staircases of a dozen steps, falls into place.
  • Stability is geography: inside the neutron-bending belt (magic addresses preferred) nuclei endure; outside, β-decays walk them home and the heavies shed α-particles.
  • Bombardment extends the map: artificial transmutation and induced radioactivity brew the isotopes that medicine and industry now order by catalogue.
  • Carbon-14 is the belt's most famous emigrant: made in the sky, eaten by everything alive, and read back as a 50 000-year clock.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (c) — Z rises by 1: one place to the right (Fajans–Soddy). Sodium's isotope β⁻-decays to magnesium, group 2.

2. (d) — light nuclei want N ≈ Z; ¹⁴C sheds the extra neutron as a β⁻ to become {}^{14}N (7,7 — near-perfect balance).

3. (a) — the signal dies exponentially under background; long clocks (K–Ar, U–Pb) take over for geology.

4. (b) — p \rightarrow n lowers Z towards the belt; which of β⁺/EC wins depends on the available energy (EC always allowed).

5. (d) — magic-Z lead sits at a local energy floor: the decay staircases (4n, 4n+2, 4n+3) terminate at Pb-208/206/207 (and Bi-209 in the extinct 4n+1).

6. (b) — induced radioactivity by neutron activation: {}^{59}Co(n,\gamma){}^{60}Co.

7. (c) — one half-life: 5730 years (after calibration refinements).

8. (a) — Coulomb repulsion is long-range (√ pair sums ∝ Z²) while strong attraction saturates with neighbours; extra neutrons add binding without adding repulsion.

9. (b) — α: Z−2, A−4; two β⁻: Z+2, A same — net same element, mass 4 less (as in Physics §20's U chain).

10. (a) — tritiated water mixes with body water (biological half-life ~10 days); low-energy β is harmless outside but must be kept from getting in (the α-particle lesson of §20.4 in reverse).

11. (d) — primordial survivors need t½ comparable to or greater than 4.5 Gyr (K-40 1.25 Gyr, U-238 4.5 Gyr, Th-232 14 Gyr).

12. (c) — a year's decay is negligible for a long t½ (or a daughter continually remade by a long-lived parent — secular equilibrium, as with radon from radium-bearing rock).
